cards.front: What is the water cycle? Name its four main stages.
cards.back: The water cycle (hydrological cycle) is the continuous movement of water through the environment. The four main stages are: (1) Evaporation — water turns into vapour due to heat. (2) Condensation — vapour cools and forms clouds. (3) Precipitation — water falls as rain, snow, or hail. (4) Collection/Infiltration — water collects in rivers, lakes, or seeps underground.
cards.memory_hook: ECPC: Every Cloud Pours Continually. Or: Evaporate → Condense → Pour (Precipitate) → Collect. The water never stops moving.

cards.front: What is evaporation? What provides the energy for it?
cards.back: Evaporation is the process by which liquid water is converted into water vapour. It occurs when water at the surface absorbs heat energy from the Sun and changes from liquid to gas. Evaporation happens continuously from oceans, rivers, lakes, wet ground, and even from sweat on your skin. The Sun is the primary energy source driving evaporation.
cards.memory_hook: Evaporate = Escape Vapour. Liquid water escapes into the air as vapour when heated. The Sun is the great escape artist, constantly turning water invisible.

cards.front: What is condensation? How does it lead to cloud formation?
cards.back: Condensation is the process by which water vapour cools and converts back into tiny liquid water droplets. When warm, moist air rises to higher altitudes, it cools. The water vapour in it condenses around tiny dust and smoke particles to form billions of tiny water droplets — these droplets together form a cloud. Dew on leaves in the morning is also condensation.
cards.memory_hook: Condensation = Cold night + steam = water on glass. Con-dens-ation = density increases (vapour becomes denser liquid). When water vapour hits something cold, it comes back as liquid.

cards.front: What is transpiration? Which part of the plant is mainly involved?
cards.back: Transpiration is the process by which plants release water vapour into the atmosphere. Plants absorb water through their roots, use some for photosynthesis, and release the rest as water vapour through tiny pores called stomata on their leaves. Transpiration from forests adds enormous amounts of water vapour to the atmosphere, contributing significantly to rainfall — this is why forested regions tend to receive more rain.
cards.memory_hook: Trans-PIRATION = plants PERSPIRING. Plants sweat through their leaves just like humans sweat through skin. A large tree can transpire 200–400 litres of water per day!

cards.front: What is precipitation? Name three forms of precipitation.
cards.back: Precipitation is the falling of water from clouds to Earth's surface in any form. Forms of precipitation: (1) Rain — liquid water droplets falling in regions where temperature is above 0°C. (2) Snow — water vapour that freezes directly into ice crystals, falling in very cold regions (mountain peaks, polar areas). (3) Sleet — a mix of rain and snow. (4) Hail — ice pellets formed when updrafts in a storm cloud repeatedly freeze water droplets before they fall.
cards.memory_hook: Precipitation = Precipitation Party: Rain dances, Snow glides, Hail drumbeats. All are water falling from clouds — just in different costumes depending on how cold it is.

cards.front: What is infiltration? Why is it important?
cards.back: Infiltration is the process by which rainwater seeps through the soil and rock to collect underground as groundwater. Infiltration is important because: (1) It recharges groundwater, which feeds wells and bore wells. (2) It filters rainwater naturally as it passes through soil. (3) It reduces surface flooding by absorbing rainwater into the ground. Permeable surfaces (soil, sand) allow good infiltration; impermeable surfaces (concrete, tar) block it.
cards.memory_hook: Infiltrate = sneak inside. Rainwater infiltrates the ground and hides underground. Concrete is the gatekeeper that stops rainwater from infiltrating — that's why cities flood more.

cards.front: What is groundwater? How is it different from surface water?
cards.back: Groundwater is water that has infiltrated through soil and collected in the pores and cracks of underground rocks and soil layers. Surface water includes water in rivers, lakes, ponds, and oceans — it is above the ground. Groundwater fills microscopic spaces in rock and soil (like water in a sponge). It is accessed through wells and bore wells. Groundwater is generally cleaner than surface water because soil acts as a natural filter.
cards.memory_hook: Surface water = visible (rivers, lakes). Groundwater = invisible underground sponge. Both come from rain — one stays on top, one sneaks underground.

cards.front: What is the water table?
cards.back: The water table is the upper level of the zone underground that is completely saturated with water (groundwater). Above the water table, the soil is unsaturated (some air in pores). Below the water table, all pores and cracks in the rock and soil are filled with water. When you dig a well, the water you find is at approximately the water table level. The water table rises after good rainfall and falls during drought or heavy extraction.
cards.memory_hook: Water TABLE = the table-top level of underground water. Dig above the table = dry. Dig below the table = wet. Monsoon raises the table; drought lowers it.

cards.front: Why do cities like Bengaluru have falling water tables despite receiving good rainfall?
cards.back: Bengaluru's rapid urbanisation has replaced permeable surfaces (soil, grassland, lakes) with impermeable surfaces (concrete roads, buildings, parking lots). When it rains, water cannot seep into the ground — instead it becomes surface runoff and flows into drains. This drastically reduces groundwater recharge, causing the water table to fall year after year. Additionally, many of Bengaluru's 280+ traditional lakes have been encroached upon, eliminating their role as recharge zones. Bore wells now need to go 800–1000 feet deep.
cards.memory_hook: Concrete = rainwater's enemy. Every new building in Bengaluru that replaces a field or lake is another nail in the water table's coffin. Concrete says: 'You can't enter.' Rain has nowhere to go but down the drain.

cards.front: What is a flood? What causes floods?
cards.back: A flood is an overflow of water beyond the normal boundaries of rivers, lakes, or sea, inundating land that is usually dry. Causes of floods: (1) Heavy or prolonged rainfall — more water than rivers can carry. (2) Deforestation — without tree roots to slow runoff, rainwater rushes quickly into rivers. (3) Urbanisation — impermeable surfaces increase runoff. (4) Dam failure or release of excess reservoir water. (5) High tides / coastal storms. Floods destroy crops, property, and lives.
cards.memory_hook: FLOOD = Full Load Of Over-incoming Data (water). Rivers get 'inbox overflow' — more water comes in than can flow out. Deforestation makes the inbox fill up faster.

cards.front: What is a drought? How is it different from a flood?
cards.back: A drought is a prolonged period of significantly below-normal rainfall, leading to shortage of water for agriculture, drinking, and industry. Floods = too much water too fast. Droughts = too little water over a long period. Effects of drought: crop failure, famine, migration, drying of wells and rivers. India's drought-prone regions include parts of Rajasthan, Maharashtra (Marathwada), and North Karnataka (Raichur, Kalaburagi). Climate change is making droughts more frequent and severe.
cards.memory_hook: Drought rhymes with 'out' — water is OUT. Like a bank account going to zero. Flood rhymes with 'flood' — the account overflows. One is empty, the other overflowing.

cards.front: How does deforestation affect the water cycle and cause both floods and droughts?
cards.back: Deforestation (cutting down forests) harms the water cycle in multiple ways: Flood effect: Tree roots absorb rainfall and slow surface runoff. Without trees, rainwater rushes rapidly over bare soil into rivers, causing flash floods. Drought effect: Less transpiration means less water vapour in the atmosphere, reducing rainfall over the region. Roots no longer hold soil moisture. Result: deforested areas often experience both more intense floods during rain and drier conditions overall. This is why the forests of Kodagu (Coorg) are critical to the health of the Cauvery river.
cards.memory_hook: Forest = Water's best friend. Forest slows rain (prevents floods), sends moisture to sky (ensures rain), holds soil and water (prevents drought). Cut forest = break all three services at once.

cards.front: What percentage of Earth's water is usable fresh water? Why is water called scarce?
cards.back: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, but 97% of it is salty ocean water, which humans cannot drink or use for most agriculture. Of the remaining 3% fresh water, about 2% is frozen in glaciers and polar ice. Only about 1% is liquid fresh water available for human use (in rivers, lakes, and groundwater). Given that 8 billion humans, all animals, and all agriculture depend on this 1%, water is genuinely scarce and precious.
cards.memory_hook: 97% salt (sea), 2% frozen (ice), 1% usable (fresh). Imagine Earth as a 100-litre tank — only 1 litre is available for all of humanity's needs. That's why every drop counts.

cards.front: What is rainwater harvesting? Describe one method.
cards.back: Rainwater harvesting is the collection, storage, and use of rainwater that would otherwise flow away as runoff. Method 1 — Rooftop harvesting: Rain falls on a clean rooftop, flows through pipes into a storage tank (for drinking/washing) or into a pit for groundwater recharge. Method 2 — Check dams: Small barriers built across streams to slow runoff and allow water to infiltrate. Method 3 — Bunding: Earthen bunds (walls) around farm fields to hold rainwater and allow it to seep in. Karnataka's BWSSB mandates rooftop rainwater harvesting for large buildings in Bengaluru.
cards.memory_hook: Harvest rain = catch it before it escapes. Just like harvesting crops (collecting what grew), rainwater harvesting collects what falls from the sky. Every rooftop is a potential water farm.

cards.front: Name five ways to conserve water in daily life.
cards.back: 1. Turn off taps while brushing teeth — saves ~6 litres/minute. 2. Fix leaking taps immediately — a leaking tap can waste thousands of litres per year. 3. Use a bucket for bathing instead of a shower — saves 50–100 litres per bath. 4. Water plants in the morning or evening (not afternoon) — less evaporation loss. 5. Use collected rice-washing water or vegetable-washing water to water plants — reusing grey water. 6. Report water wastage in public places. Each person saving even 10 litres/day = millions of litres saved collectively.
cards.memory_hook: TAP: Turn off, Avoid leaks, Pour wisely. Every time you turn off a running tap, you save a litre. Small acts × 8 billion people = enormous water savings.

cards.front: What is a kere (Karnataka traditional tank)? Why are they important?
cards.back: A kere is a traditional rainwater storage tank (pond) built in Karnataka villages and towns over centuries. Kere are small reservoirs built by digging or constructing earthen bunds to collect monsoon runoff. They serve multiple purposes: drinking and domestic water, irrigation, recharging groundwater (water seeps from kere into surrounding soil), and supporting local biodiversity. Karnataka has over 35,000 traditional kere — many have been encroached upon by urbanisation. Reviving kere is an important water conservation strategy today.
cards.memory_hook: Kere = Karnataka's ancient water bank. For centuries, villages deposited their monsoon rain 'income' in kere and withdrew water during the dry season. Encroaching on kere = destroying your own bank.

cards.front: Why do forests receive more rainfall than open land?
cards.back: Forests receive more rainfall because: (1) Transpiration: Trees release large amounts of water vapour, increasing atmospheric moisture. (2) Interception and evaporation: Leaves intercept rain, which evaporates slowly and cools the air, triggering more rain. (3) Soil: Forest soil has good structure that allows water infiltration — this water is later released slowly. Forested hills (like the Western Ghats in Karnataka) act as 'rain catchers' — the moisture-laden sea winds rise over the Ghats, cool, and release heavy rainfall on the western slopes.
cards.memory_hook: Forest = Rain Magnet. Trees literally make more rain by putting water vapour back into the sky. Cut the forest, lose the rain. The Western Ghats prove this — dense forest = 3000+ mm rain.

cards.front: Why do we find dew on leaves early in the morning?
cards.back: During the day, water evaporates from the ground, plants, and water bodies, adding water vapour to the air. At night, the air and surfaces (especially leaves) cool down significantly. When the leaf surface temperature drops below the dew point (the temperature at which air can no longer hold its water vapour), the water vapour in the air condenses on the cool leaf surfaces as tiny water droplets — this is dew. Dew is a form of condensation, exactly like water droplets forming on a cold glass of water on a humid day.
cards.memory_hook: Dew = Night's condensation gift. Warm day → lots of vapour in air → cold night → vapour condenses on cool leaves = dew. Your cold water glass in summer does the same thing.

cards.front: The Cauvery river originates in Karnataka. How is the water cycle connected to the river's flow?
cards.back: The Cauvery river originates at Talacauvery in Kodagu (Coorg) district, which receives 3000–5000 mm of rainfall annually during the Southwest Monsoon (June–September). This rainfall: (1) Falls as precipitation on the Western Ghats forests. (2) Some infiltrates into the ground and feeds springs that flow year-round. (3) Surface runoff collects in streams that join to form the Cauvery river. (4) Transpiration from Kodagu's forests maintains the moisture cycle and ensures continued rainfall. Thus the water cycle — specifically precipitation, infiltration, and surface runoff — directly feeds the Cauvery. Deforestation in Kodagu threatens the river's flow.
cards.memory_hook: Rain in Kodagu → Cauvery flows → KRS dam fills → Bengaluru and Mysuru drink. Every shower in Bengaluru started as monsoon rain in a Coorg forest, filtered through the water cycle.

cards.front: How is the water cycle demonstrated by boiling water in a pot with a lid?
cards.back: Boiling water with a lid is a miniature water cycle: (1) Evaporation: Heat from the stove causes water in the pot to evaporate — steam rises (water vapour). (2) Condensation: Steam (water vapour) hits the cooler lid, cools, and condenses into water droplets on the inside surface of the lid. (3) Precipitation: The droplets grow heavy and drip back down into the pot (like rain). This is exactly the water cycle: Sun (stove) heats water → evaporation → vapour rises → hits cooler surface (lid/atmosphere) → condenses → falls back as liquid.
cards.memory_hook: Kitchen pot = Earth's water cycle in 5 minutes. Stove = Sun. Lid = atmosphere. Steam = evaporation. Drips from lid = rain. Next time you cook, you're watching a model of the water cycle.
